glossary.definition: The role responsible for decisions and records in the defined workflow.
A point where a record moves from one person or system to another.
Statements the team can test when judging software.
What an auditor saw, read or was told, recorded in enough detail for someone else to check.
A requirement, procedure or stated expectation against which evidence is measured.
A judgment drawn from observations and measured against criteria.
Statements of the evidence, checker and timing required for a finding's follow-up.
An import using a limited, representative set of records to reveal problems before a wider import.
The point at which the new system becomes the working record.
Planning what would trigger a rollback and how it would work.
A test of whether representative users can perform work in the system with the relevant records and constraints.
Introducing groups of users or parts of the audit program in a planned order.
The level of audit planning that covers the period as a whole.
The level of planning for a single audit.

example.label: Illustrative example
example.description: An unnamed Canadian manufacturer evaluates internal audit management software for one production workflow; all situations and records are hypothetical, not customer results.

reviewedChapters.title: Mapping the current workflow: Internal audit management software
reviewedChapters.summary: The page follows the assigned workflow, distinguishes sourced claims from advice and hypothetical examples, and stays within the chapter boundary. No FAQ is assigned or included.
decisions: Which workflow break to solve first and whether to accept the problem statement.
How to handle missing records or disagreements about the authoritative record.
Which records are authoritative, copies, or working notes, and whether to accept the record map.
How to handle records without a clear owner or stored in a personal location.
Which roles own handoffs and decisions, including primary and backup owners.
How to handle unfilled roles, conflicts of interest, or unreachable owners.
Which acceptance criteria are must-haves, should-haves, or could-haves and what counts as a pass.
How to handle criteria that cannot be tested or conflict with each other.

reviewedChapters.title: Evaluating software capabilities: Internal audit management software
reviewedChapters.summary: The changed paragraph presents a provisional recommendation and final approval without introducing a clear problem. No earlier findings remain unresolved.
decisions: Which candidates proceed to demonstration and whether to request a trial for a missing must-have demonstration.
Whether each test scenario passed, failed, or was not shown, and how to handle a scenario that cannot be run live.
Whether permissions enforce the team's separation rules and how to handle an unenforceable rule.
Which product to recommend, how to address missing cost or support information, and whether to approve the recommendation.

reviewedChapters.title: Planning the internal audit program: Internal audit management software
reviewedChapters.summary: The changed paragraphs present no clear problems, and there are no earlier findings to resolve. No FAQ is assigned or included.
decisions: Accept or return the program and individual audit scopes; resolve or escalate scope disputes.
Accept or reject auditor assignments and decide how to handle an unavailable impartial auditor.
Accept or return the calendar and decide how to respond when an area is unavailable.
Accept or reject changes to move, add or cancel audits, including short-notice requests.

reviewedChapters.title: Collecting and connecting audit evidence: Internal audit management software
reviewedChapters.summary: The changed paragraph presents a practical offline test and fallback without introducing a clear problem. No previous findings remain unresolved.
decisions: Accept or return the checklist and decide how to handle unsuitable or disputed questions.
Accept or reject the observation recording method and decide how to handle unavailable connectivity or devices.
Accept or return evidence-to-criterion links and decide how to address evidence without a criterion or a criterion without evidence.
Approve access rules and accept or return their configuration after testing.
Grant, narrow or refuse temporary access and record the disposition of an unenforceable rule.

decisions: Whether an observation becomes a finding and which category applies.
Whether evidence supports a finding or the finding should be returned, held or withdrawn.
Who owns the response and when it is due.
Whether a disputed finding stands, is revised, is withdrawn or is held for more evidence.
Who independently reviews and accepts a dispute decision when the quality manager is involved.

reviewedChapters.title: Following findings through closure: Internal audit management software

decisions: Approve or return follow-up criteria and resolve findings that fit no criterion.

Close, hold or keep a finding open based on required effectiveness checks.

reviewedChapters.title: Planning migration and configuration: Internal audit management software

decisions: Classify each record type and accept or return the inventory; assign an owner and interim class when ownership or retention is unclear.

Accept the pilot, rerun it or progress with a documented gap approved by top management.
Approve or postpone cutover and decide whether to roll back or continue with an approved, documented gap.

reviewedChapters.title: Internal audit management software for Canadian quality and operations teams
reviewedChapters.summary: The introduction covers the assigned scope, gives an ordered guide overview, uses supported sources and labels its examples as hypothetical. No FAQ was assigned or included.
decisions: Who schedules audits, who may close findings, and what evidence is acceptable.
Which problem and acceptance criteria will guide the software evaluation.
Which roles own workflow decisions and project stages.
Whether to proceed, repeat or stop at each project stage.
How to set audit frequency, duration and scope.
How to assign auditors and change the schedule when production or risk changes.
How to classify and confirm findings and handle disputes.
What follow-up is required and when a finding should be reopened.
How to migrate records, configure the system, train users and deploy it.
How to measure success and review improvements using the team's own records.
